title: ¿Por qué git checkout no puede deshacer lo que cambió un agente de IA en tu código?
author: Hanako H.
summary: Cuando un agente de IA edita archivos de tu proyecto y rompe algo, el reflejo es git checkout -- . o git stash . Los dos responden a una pregunta distinta de la que tienes. Git puede llevarte al último commit. Lo que quieres es la carpeta tal como estaba justo antes del turno del agente, con tu propio trabajo sin commitear y los archivos que git ignora, y sin los archivos que creó el agente. La aplicación de escritorio de osFoundry lo resuelve con un pequeño almacén direccionado por contenido escrito en Rust, checkpoint_store.rs . Antes de que una escritura del agente llegue a un archivo, los bytes actuales del archivo se guardan en <project>/.osfoundry/checkpoints/blobs/<sha256> , y /rewind los vuelve a escribir. Aquí tienes el mismo diseño en unas 90 líneas de Python con solo la biblioteca estándar, comparado con cuatro recetas de git sobre un turno realista y cronometrado sobre una copia de un árbol de código TypeScript real de 4,686 archivos. Un turno, cinco formas de deshacerlo El proyecto de prueba es un sitio diminuto en un repositorio git: index.html , styles.css (212 líneas), app.js y un .env que .gitignore excluye. Después del último commit, el usuario cambió el título de la página en index.html y empezó un notes.md sin seguimiento. Ese es el estado al que hay que volver. Luego viene el turno del agente: reescribe styles.css hasta dejarlo en 41 líneas, edita index.html para cargar un nuevo theme.css , reescribe app.js , apunta API_URL en .env a localhost y crea theme.css . Cada método de deshacer se ejecutó sobre una copia limpia, y un script comparó cada archivo byte a byte con el estado anterior al turno. checkpoint restore matches the state before the turn: True differs: [] git checkout -- . matches the state before the turn: False differs: ['.env', 'index.html', 'theme.css'] git stash -u matches the state before the turn: False differs: ['.env', 'index.html', 'notes.md'] git checkout + git clean -fd matches the state before the turn: False differs: ['.env', 'index.html', 'notes.md'] git stash create before the turn matches the state before the turn: False differs: ['.env', 'theme.css'] Método Qué sale mal git checkout -- . La edición del título del usuario se pierde junto con las del agente, theme.css se queda y .env conserva el valor del agente git stash -u Los cambios del agente, la edición del título del usuario y notes.md acaban juntos en un mismo stash, y .env conserva el valor del agente git checkout + git clean -fd theme.css se elimina, pero notes.md también, la edición del título desaparece y .env conserva el valor del agente git stash create antes del turno Todo lo que tiene seguimiento vuelve, pero theme.css se queda y .env nunca entra en la instantánea restauración del checkpoint Coincide con el estado anterior al turno Los resultados de git se deducen de lo que es git. Restaura el último commit, o una instantánea de los archivos con seguimiento y en staging, y ambas cosas mezclan tu trabajo con el del agente en cuanto ninguno de los dos está commiteado. Los archivos ignorados le resultan invisibles salvo que añadas -a , y un checkout nunca borra un archivo que no existía en la instantánea. La última fila es la configuración de git más justa, una instantánea tomada antes de cada turno, y aun así falla en dos de los cinco archivos. Además tiene un efecto secundario: git add -A pone en staging todo tu trabajo en el índice real en cada turno. El almacén Un checkpoint es una lista por turno: para cada archivo que escribió el agente, o bien el hash de su contenido anterior, o bien una nota de que no existía. Los bytes van a blobs/ una sola vez por cada contenido distinto. import hashlib , json , os , time from pathlib import Path MAX_BLOB = 8 * 1024 * 1024 class Checkpoints : def __init__ ( self , root ): self . root = Path ( root ). resolve () self . dir = self . root / " .osfoundry " / " checkpoints " self . blobs = self . dir / " blobs " self . index_file = self . dir / " index.json " try : self . index = json . loads ( self . index_file . read_text ()) except ( OSError , ValueError ): self . index = [] def _save ( self ): self . dir . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) tmp = self . dir / " index.json.tmp " tmp . write_text ( json . dumps ( self . index )) os . replace ( tmp , self . index_file ) # a half-written index loses everything def capture ( self , turn , label , path ): path = str ( Path ( path ). resolve ()) if Path ( path ). exists () else str ( Path ( path ). absolute ()) if not self . _contained ( path ): raise ValueError ( " outside the workspace: " + path ) cp = next (( c for c in self . index if c [ " turn " ] == turn ), None ) if cp and any ( f [ " path " ] == path for f in cp [ " files " ]): return # first write in a turn wins try : size = os . path . getsize ( path ) except FileNotFoundError : pre = { " kind " : " absent " } else : if size > MAX_BLOB : pre = { " kind " : " skipped " , " reason " : f " { size >> 20 } MB over the limit " } else : data = Path ( path ). read_bytes () sha = hashlib . sha256 ( data ). hexdigest () blob = self . blobs / sha if not blob . exists (): # identical bytes are stored once self . blobs . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) blob . write_bytes ( data ) pre = { " kind " : " content " , " sha256 " : sha , " bytes " : size } entry = { " path " : path , " pre " : pre } if cp : cp [ " files " ]. append ( entry ) else : self . index . append ({ " turn " : turn , " label " : label [: 120 ], " at " : time . time_ns (), " files " : [ entry ]}) self . _save () def write ( self , turn , label , path , data ): """ What an agent ' s write tool would call. """ self . capture ( turn , label , path ) Path ( path ). parent . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) Path ( path ). write_bytes ( data ) Tres detalles deciden si una restauración es correcta, y cada uno es también una regla en el módulo de Rust. Gana la primera captura de una ruta en un turno. Un agente escribe a menudo el mismo archivo varias veces en un turno. Rebobinar significa volver a cómo estaba el archivo cuando empezó el turno, no a algún estado entre dos escrituras del propio agente, así que las capturas posteriores de la misma ruta en el mismo turno se ignoran. Un archivo que no existe se registra como absent . Esa única línea es lo que permite que una restauración borre theme.css . Git no tiene equivalente para "este archivo no debe existir", salvo un git clean que también borra archivos que querías conservar. Los archivos de más de 8 MB se registran como skipped con un motivo, no se omiten. Así, una restauración informa de que no pudo devolverlos, en lugar de terminar en silencio con una mezcla de archivos viejos y nuevos. Restaurar, del más antiguo al más reciente def restore ( self , turn ): target = next ( c [ " at " ] for c in self . index if c [ " turn " ] == turn ) affected = sorted (( c for c in self . index if c [ " at " ] >= target ), key = lambda c : c [ " at " ]) # oldest first done , report = set (), { " restored " : [], " deleted " : [], " failed " : []} for cp in affected : for f in cp [ " files " ]: path , pre = f [ " path " ], f [ " pre " ] if path in done : continue done . add ( path ) if not self . _contained ( path ): # re-check, the index is just a file report [ " failed " ]. append (( path , " outside the workspace " )) elif pre [ " kind " ] == " skipped " : report [ " failed " ]. append (( path , pre [ " reason " ])) elif pre [ " kind " ] == " absent " : Path ( path ). unlink ( missing_ok = True ) report [ " deleted " ]. append ( path ) else : Path ( path ). parent . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) Path ( path ). write_bytes (( self . blobs / pre [ " sha256 " ]). read_bytes ()) report [ " restored " ]. append ( path ) self . index = [ c for c in self . index if c [ " at " ] < target ] self . _save () return report def _contained ( self , path ): p = Path ( path ) if " .. " in p . parts : return False p = p if p . is_absolute () else self . root / p while not p . exists (): # deepest existing ancestor, symlinks resolved p = p . parent return p . resolve (). is_relative_to ( self . root ) Rebobinar el turno 1 cuando después vinieron los turnos 2 y 3 debe deshacer los tres. Restaurar solo el turno 1 dejaría archivos del turno 2 junto a archivos de antes del turno 1, una combinación que nunca existió. El orden también importa. Para un archivo tocado en varios turnos, los bytes correctos son la preimagen más antigua, la que se capturó cuando empezó el turno 1. Recorrer del más reciente al más antiguo acaba en la preimagen del turno 2, que es el estado que produjo el turno 1. El código Rust tiene un comentario justo sobre esto: al principio se escribió del más reciente al más antiguo, y el test rewinding_a_turn_also_undoes_later_turns lo detectó. La comprobación de la ruta se repite al restaurar porque index.json es un archivo normal dentro de la carpeta que describe. Si se confiara en él, cualquiera o cualquier cosa capaz de editarlo podría hacer que una restauración escribiera en cualquier parte del disco. Después, los turnos rebobinados se eliminan del índice, para que un segundo rebobinado al mismo punto no pueda "tener éxito" sobre archivos que ya están de vuelta. Cuánto cuesta en una carpeta real El árbol es una copia de la carpeta src de una app real de React y TypeScript: 4,686 archivos, 121.4 MB, ninguno de más de 8 MB. En cada turno se eligieron archivos al azar, se capturaron y se les añadió una línea; luego se ejecutó una restauración y se comparó cada archivo con el original. Todas las restauraciones coincidieron. Apple M1, 8 GB, macOS 15, SSD con APFS, Python 3.9.6, git 2.39.5. Turno Captura + escritura Tamaño del almacén Restauración 4 archivos + 1 creado 3.5 ms menos de 0.1 MB 1.2 ms 50 archivos + 1 creado 62.4 ms 0.9 MB 8.2 ms 500 archivos + 1 creado 1,035 ms 11.7 MB 227 ms los 4,686 archivos 30.5 s 122.7 MB 1.3 s Para comparar, la instantánea de git por turno del escenario anterior ( git add -A y luego git stash create ) tardó entre 61 y 68 ms en este árbol sin ningún cambio, y entre 50 y 67 ms con cuatro archivos editados. Tiene que mirar los 4,686 archivos cada vez. Justo después de la ejecución que reescribió todos los archivos, la siguiente tardó 1,241 ms, porque git vuelve a calcular el hash de cada archivo cuya marca de tiempo cambió. Un checkpoint solo mira los archivos que se están escribiendo, así que un turno normal cuesta unos pocos milisegundos sea cual sea el tamaño del proyecto. La última fila deja ver un problema en el código tal como está. La captura media tardó 1.29 ms en los primeros 100 archivos del turno y 9.54 ms en los últimos 100. Cada captura reescribe el index.json entero, que llegó a 1.3 MB, así que el coste de cada escritura crece con el número de escrituras anteriores. Sustituir _save por un append de una línea JSON por captura lo arregló con los mismos 4,686 archivos: 2.5 s en total, 0.41 ms por captura al principio y 0.61 ms al final. Para un agente que edita unos pocos archivos por turno, la versión simple basta. Para un formateador o un renombrado en todo el código ejecutado a través de un agente, usa el log de solo append. Lo que ahorra el direccionamiento por contenido, y lo que no Nombrar los blobs por su SHA-256 deduplica los bytes idénticos y nada más. Tres mediciones muestran dónde queda eso. En todo el árbol, 4,686 archivos tenían 4,677 contenidos distintos, así que un turno sobre el árbol completo guardó 4,677 blobs. Los archivos duplicados son raros en un árbol de código real. Un archivo de 2 MB reescrito en diez turnos, con el agente añadiendo una línea cada vez: diez preimágenes, todas distintas, 10 blobs y 20.0 MB. El mismo archivo, pero el agente escribe los mismos bytes en cada turno, como hace un reintento que produce una salida idéntica: 2 blobs y 4.0 MB, el original y la versión desde la que partió cada turno posterior. En los dos casos, rebobinar al primer turno devolvió el original byte a byte. Los blobs se guardan sin comprimir. Los 121.4 MB de blobs del turno sobre el árbol completo serían 33.7 MB con zlib a nivel 6, y el propio almacén de objetos de git para el mismo árbol tras un commit ocupaba 41.0 MB. La compresión es un añadido razonable si el almacén se conserva mucho tiempo, ya que el código fuente se comprime aproximadamente 3.6 a 1. Los deltas entre versiones, como en los pack files de git, ahorrarían más en el caso de añadir una línea, pero cuestan mucho más código del que necesita un almacén de preimágenes. Límites de esta versión Solo ve las escrituras que pasan por write() . Si tu agente también puede ejecutar comandos de shell, un rm o un sed -i se le escapan por completo. La aplicación de osFoundry hace pasar las escrituras de archivos del agente por una sola función, que es donde captura. Una restauración escribe la preimagen sin importar lo que haya ahora en el archivo. Si editaste un archivo a mano después del agente, rebobinar ese turno también reemplaza tu edición. Una versión más estricta registra el hash de lo que escribió el agente y, antes de restaurar, comprueba si el archivo sigue teniendo ese hash. Si no, guarda primero los bytes actuales como un blob más, de modo que también se pueda deshacer la restauración. Además, el almacén crece hasta que se rebobinan turnos. Basta con un prune que borre los blobs a los que no hace referencia ningún checkpoint, más un límite de cuántos turnos conservar. Los dos bloques de la clase de arriba son el almacén completo, Python 3.9 con la biblioteca estándar y nada que instalar. La aplicación de escritorio de osFoundry incluye la versión en Rust como /rewind en los chats que trabajan en una carpeta local , gratis desde la página de descarga de osFoundry .

title: Mistral's New Agents SDK Runs Tool Calls Without Asking by Default. Set a Policy First
author: Gabriel Anhaia
summary: Book: RAG Pocket Guide The series: Pocket Guides for Developers — 8 short books on agents, RAG, prompts, observability, events, databases and system design — the whole series My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub You give your new agent two tools: one that reads an alert, one that opens an incident case. You never wrote an approval rule, so you assume it will ask before it opens anything. With Mistral's new Agents SDK, it won't. The default permission_mode is "auto" , which Mistral's approvals docs define as: "follows the permission_policy , or runs when the Agent has none." That SDK is the center of the Studio release Mistral shipped on November 5 : twelve release-note entries, almost all of them public previews. What shipped on November 5 The headline item in the release notes is Managed Agents: build an agent in Python with the Agents SDK, then run the same code on your own machines or on Mistral's infrastructure. The same day brought a workflow builder, an Apps CLI, an evaluation SDK, managed datasets, a managed search index, tracing for managed agents, webhooks and online evaluations. Mistral's announcement leads with Mistral Large 4, nicknamed "Le Chonk," and lists skills, sandboxes, subagents and hooks as the building blocks of an agent. AlphaSignal's write-up adds the availability split: Managed Agents and Apps are in public preview on Mistral Cloud, and Workflows itself is generally available (the new builder is in preview). AlphaSignal also reports private-cloud and on-premises options at the end of November; Mistral's own pages don't give a date. The Agents overview is blunt about the stage: "Managed Agents and the Agents SDK are in public preview," and the API, behavior and limits may change in ways that need code changes. Pin the version. One agent, three places to run it The SDK ships as mistralai-agents . The quickstart needs Python 3.12, 3.13 or 3.14, the standard build and not free-threaded 3.14t, and pins the version in its own example: uv init --python 3.12 my_agent && cd my_agent uv add "mistralai-agents==1.1.0" export MISTRAL_API_KEY = "<your-key>" The smallest agent in the overview is five lines: import asyncio from mistralai import agents agent = agents . Agent ( model = " mistral-large-4 " ) result = asyncio . run ( agent . run ( " Say hello " )) print ( result . text ) From there, per the overview , the same code runs three ways. In-process, the harness, tools and session live in your program and end with it. With agents serve , the harness and your tools run on your servers and Mistral stores the session. With agents deploy , everything runs on Mistral and you "host nothing." One agent definition, three runtimes: your process, your servers, or Mistral's. Two deploy details are easy to miss. The deploy guide says agents deploy "builds the commit you pushed, not your working copy," and it refuses unpushed commits and branches without an upstream. And check your plan. Mistral's managed-deployment quotas , documented in the Workflows section, allow 0 concurrent deployments on Free and on Pro or Team without pay-as-you-go, 3 with pay-as-you-go, and 10 on Enterprise. Past the cap, creating or starting a deployment fails with a 403 . Managed deployments cover agents, workflows and apps, so expect the same caps on agents deploy . The default: your tools just run An agent with no permission_policy and the default permission_mode="auto" runs every tool call it decides to make. The other two modes are "ask" and "deny" ( approvals docs ). For anything that writes, add a policy. This one is Mistral's own example from the approvals page, rewrapped to fit, with the variable renamed to policy : policy = agents . PermissionPolicy ( default = " deny " , rules = [ agents . PermissionRule ( tools = [ " client.get_alert " ], decision = " allow " ), # opening a case asks agents . PermissionRule ( tools = [ " client.open_case " ], decision = " ask " ), ], ) Building the policy changes nothing until the agent gets it: agent = agents . Agent ( model = " mistral-large-4 " , permission_policy = policy , ) Three rules from the same page decide whether it does what you think. The first matching rule wins. A call that matches no rule gets the policy's default , so default="deny" is what turns this into an allowlist. And patterns match the tool ID, such as client.open_case , not the name the model sees. Check the IDs your agent actually reports before you trust a rule. A policy also needs permission_mode="auto" ; the Agent raises an error with any other mode. With no policy, every call goes through. A deny-by-default policy lets through only what you listed. Approval requests can be answered in code. An on_approval= callback returns AllowApproval() , DenyApproval() or KeepCallbackOpen() , and the last one leaves the call to a person. Mistral's own example auto-approves calls whose tool carries a read_only_hint annotation and hands everything else to a human ( approvals docs ). The defaults Mistral did get right Give the SDK its due. Several defaults fail closed. An agent has no environment unless you give it one. The default is NoSandbox , which the environment docs describe as "no code execution." When you add one, the page recommends MistralSandbox , a Mistral-managed container. The option with no isolation at all, DangerousLocalSandbox , won't start unless you set ALLOW_DANGEROUS_LOCAL_HOST=1 . If you only need file edits, access="files" gives the model read_file , write_file and edit and removes bash : agent = agents . Agent ( model = " mistral-large-4 " , environment = agents . MistralSandbox ( access = " files " ), ) A call nobody approves doesn't run either. It waits one hour, and then, per the approvals docs , "the call does not run, the model reads that nobody approved it, and the turn continues." A deployed session ends after 4 hours idle or 24 hours in total by default, per the session lifecycle page , and a session ended by a limit can't resume. On Mistral-managed deployments you can raise those to 24 hours idle and a week total; with agents serve , both go up to a year. If your agent waits on a human over a weekend, plan for a new session. Subagents need one more check. They "run in the root's sandbox and share its files," according to the subagents page , with at most 10 subagent turns at once and a tree two levels deep. The subagent approvals page has the catch for the policy above: "A default="deny" policy has no rule for agents.spawn , the tool that starts a subagent. Every start is denied." If you use subagents, add an allow or ask rule for agents.spawn . One on_approval handler answers approvals for the whole tree, so write it for every tool a subagent might call. The search index leaves chunking to you The managed search index is the other piece agents will lean on. The release notes describe it as "a hosted vector index from a name, an embedding model, and an optional schema." The Search Index overview says it supports vector, keyword and hybrid retrieval with filters, and is also in public preview. Mistral hosts the index. Per the same page, your pipeline still splits content into chunks, embeds them and sends them with their fields. The Search Toolkit supplies splitting and embedding components. Whether your agent finds the right clause depends on the chunk boundaries you pick. Tracing is on by default for managed agents. The release notes say agent, model and tool spans go to Studio with no extra package to install, and "Spans are redacted on the worker before they leave." Read what the redaction covers before you send customer data through a tool. I haven't run the SDK myself. Everything above comes from Mistral's docs and announcement as of November 6, plus AlphaSignal's write-up for the availability split. Before your first agents deploy , check the tool IDs your agent reports and write the deny policy against those IDs. Do you want agent SDKs to ask before every write by default, or is allow-by-default the right call for a developer tool? Tell me in the comments. If this was useful If you also work with Claude Code or Codex, I build Hermes IDE , an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools. It's source-available (BSL 1.1) and runs on macOS, Windows and Linux; weigh the mention with that in mind, and star it on GitHub if it helps. Mistral will host your vector index, but it still leaves chunking, embedding and retrieval quality to you. The RAG Pocket Guide covers that part: how to chunk, when to rerank, and how to tell whether retrieval is the reason an agent answered wrong. It's one of 8 short books in the Pocket Guides for Developers series , on agents, RAG, prompts, observability, events, databases and system design.

title: The Blindfolded Hike That Explains How Machines Learn
author: Sohaib Hassan
summary: Picture this: someone blindfolds you halfway up a hillside and asks you to find the lowest point. You cannot see a thing. All you can do is feel which way the ground tilts under your shoes, take one step, and feel again. That exact walk is what every machine learning model performs, over and over, while it is being trained. Its hillside is just built out of numbers instead of rocks and grass. By the end of this post you will understand that walk well enough to read it in code, not just picture it. What a model is actually doing when it "learns" Say you are building a model to guess house prices. You feed it a house, and it spits out a number: maybe $300,000. The real price was $340,000. Your model was wrong by $40,000. That wrongness has a name: a loss function (sometimes called a cost function). It is one number that says how bad the current guess is. Zero means a perfect guess. A model's guess is controlled by adjustable numbers inside it, called parameters or weights. Learning means searching for parameter values that make the loss as small as possible, across every example the model has seen. Plot the loss as a graph, with height meaning "how wrong," and you get an imaginary hillside. The lowest point is the best the model can do. The slope under your feet, which direction makes the loss grow fastest and by how much, is called the gradient. Put it together: gradient descent means feel the slope, step downhill, feel again, repeat, until you cannot go down any further. In one line of pseudocode: parameters = parameters - step_size * gradient(loss, parameters) Why step size changes everything Tiny steps are safe but slow. Giant steps can overshoot the bottom entirely and land you worse off than where you started, then overshoot again on the way back. The chart above is a real, computed run starting five units from the bottom. A step size of 0.05 is still almost two units away after ten steps. A step size of 0.30 settles near zero in about five steps. A step size of 1.05 never settles, it swings further out with every step. Here is a tiny, runnable version of the "just right" line from that chart, using plain f(x) = x^2 as the loss: def loss ( x ): return x ** 2 def gradient ( x ): return 2 * x x = 5.0 step_size = 0.3 for step in range ( 1 , 7 ): x = x - step_size * gradient ( x ) print ( f " step { step } : x = { x : . 4 f } , loss = { loss ( x ) : . 4 f } " ) Real output: step 1: x = 2.0000, loss = 4.0000 step 2: x = 0.8000, loss = 0.6400 step 3: x = 0.3200, loss = 0.1024 step 4: x = 0.1280, loss = 0.0164 step 5: x = 0.0512, loss = 0.0026 step 6: x = 0.0205, loss = 0.0004 Every optimizer you have ever passed to a training loop, SGD, Adam, RMSProp, is some descendant of this same loop, with extra bookkeeping added to make the steps faster or steadier. I built my students a window into this hill I teach advanced mathematics and statistics, and gradient descent is one of those ideas that looks simple on a whiteboard and still leaves students stuck. So I animated it in Manim, the same engine behind 3Blue1Brown's videos, building a full visual proof of exactly how fast gradient descent is guaranteed to converge, worked through on a real example. Where the 1/k guarantee comes from In that video, the walker starts 4 units from the bottom. The hill is smooth: its slope never changes faster than a fixed rate L, here L = 1, so step size 1/L = 1 is mathematically safe. x next ​ = x current ​ − (step size) × (slope at x current ​ ) Walking it out: 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, the bottom reached in exactly four steps. The error after each step: 2.5, 1.5, 0.5, 0. Because the hill is smooth and convex (shaped like a single bowl with one lowest point), there is a proven ceiling on the error after k steps: error after k steps ≤ k 8 ​ That bound decays like "one over k": roughly ten times more steps for ten times more accuracy. This method is not new either. Augustin-Louis Cauchy described it in a short note in 1847, while computing a star's orbit using algebra instead of harder equations by hand. Where this breaks down Real loss surfaces are rarely one clean bowl. A model can land in a shallow dip, a local minimum, and stop there even though a deeper valley exists elsewhere. Picking L exactly, the way we did above, only works because the example was simple. Real step sizes are usually tuned through experiment instead. And a real model's hill has one direction per parameter, sometimes millions of them, which is exactly why plain gradient descent gets replaced by its smarter cousins at scale. One line to take with you Every model that has ever learned anything has done nothing more than take small, careful steps downhill until it could not go any lower, the same walk Cauchy described in 1847, just running in a training loop instead of an astronomer's notebook. Words used in this post Gradient descent: a method for finding the lowest point of a hill of numbers by repeatedly stepping downhill. Loss function (cost function): a single number that measures how wrong a model's current guess is. Parameter (weight): one of the adjustable numbers inside a model that changes its guesses. Learning rate: how big a step the model takes downhill at each try. Local minimum: a dip in the hill that looks like the bottom but is not the lowest point overall. Convergence: the point where the steps stop improving the guess by any meaningful amount. Convex: shaped like a single smooth bowl, with exactly one lowest point. title: Image Trace vs an AI Vectorizer: Count the Paths, Not the Label
author: PerfectVector
summary: "Image Trace or an AI vectorizer?" usually gets answered with labels: one is built into Illustrator, the other says AI on the box. Both do the same job, rebuilding a raster image as vector paths. Adobe documents Image Trace's presets and its controls for paths, corners, noise and colors in the Image Trace panel guide , but not enough of the implementation to say which approach is "more AI". The label tells you little. The expanded output tells you a lot. Workflow is the honest split. If you already edit in Illustrator and like hand-tuning a trace before you expand it, Image Trace is right there. If you want an automated result without opening a design app, or you need an API or batch surface (some dedicated tools have one, so check the docs), test a dedicated vectorizer. Neither turns a photo into a clean SVG: continuous tone comes back as posterized art or thousands of shapes, and no tracer invents detail a low-res source never captured. What decides your cleanup time is the paths: how many segments the same shape needs, whether you can select and recolor one region instead of a welded tangle, and whether the silhouette still matches the source. So trace the same image in both, at the same intended fidelity, and put a number on it. This dependency-free script counts the drawing segments in a plain SVG: import re , sys ARGS = dict ( m = 2 , l = 2 , h = 1 , v = 1 , c = 6 , s = 4 , q = 4 , t = 2 , a = 7 , z = 0 ) TOKEN = re . compile ( r " [MmLlHhVvCcSsQqTtAaZz]|[-+]?(?:\d*\.\d+|\d+\.?)(?:[eE][-+]?\d+)? " ) def segments ( d ): """ Count drawing segments in one path ' s d attribute, implicit repeats included. """ count , cmd , nums = 0 , None , 0 for tok in TOKEN . findall ( d ) + [ " Z " ]: if tok . isalpha (): if cmd and ARGS [ cmd ]: count += nums // ARGS [ cmd ] - ( cmd == " m " ) # extra M pairs are lines cmd , nums = tok . lower (), 0 else : nums += 1 return count svg = open ( sys . argv [ 1 ], encoding = " utf-8 " ). read () paths = re . findall ( r " <path\b[^>]*?\sd=[\" ' ]([^\" ' ]*) " , svg ) images = len ( re . findall ( r " <image\b " , svg )) print ( f " { len ( paths ) } paths, { sum ( map ( segments , paths )) } segments, { images } embedded images " ) Run python count_nodes.py trace-a.svg and python count_nodes.py trace-b.svg , then put both files side by side at the same zoom. Fewer segments for the same silhouette means easier edits and lighter files downstream; a non-zero "embedded images" count means part of the file is still a bitmap. The script reads <path> elements only (shapes like <circle> are skipped), doesn't count the implicit closing line of z , and expects arc flags separated by spaces or commas. On a 60-path test file it matched svgpathtools' segment count exactly. title: Compress images from Python with the Blinkimg API and requests
author: Sahadat Husain
summary: To compress an image from Python with the Blinkimg API you make four HTTP calls with requests : ask for an upload slot, PUT the bytes, create a job, then read the result link. The client below is 40 lines with no SDK. In my run it turned a 576.8 KB JPEG into a 93.9 KB AVIF with targetBytes: 100000 . What does the API flow look like? The API has three endpoints you need, under https://api.blinkimg.com/v1 : POST /v1/uploads with filename and contentLength . It answers with an uploadId and a signed url . You PUT the file to that url . POST /v1/jobs with the uploadId and an options object: format , quality or targetBytes , resize , stripMetadata . GET /v1/jobs/{id} until status leaves queued and processing , then GET /v1/jobs/{id}/result for a signed link to the file. Every call carries Authorization: Bearer <key> . You create the key from your account; the API docs list the endpoints and the OpenAPI description. The whole client import os , sys , time , uuid from pathlib import Path import requests API = os . environ . get ( " BLINKIMG_API " , " https://api.blinkimg.com/v1 " ) session = requests . Session () session . headers [ " Authorization " ] = f " Bearer { os . environ [ ' BLINKIMG_KEY ' ] } " class BlinkimgError ( Exception ): pass def call ( method , path , ** kw ): r = session . request ( method , f " { API }{ path } " , timeout = 30 , ** kw ) if r . status_code >= 400 : err = r . json (). get ( " error " , {}) raise BlinkimgError ( f " { r . status_code } { err . get ( ' code ' ) } : { err . get ( ' message ' ) } " ) return r . json () def compress ( src : Path , dest_dir : Path , ** options ) -> dict : data = src . read_bytes () # 1. an upload slot, then the bytes straight to storage (no auth header there) upload = call ( " POST " , " /uploads " , json = { " filename " : src . name , " contentLength " : len ( data )}) requests . put ( upload [ " url " ], data = data , timeout = 60 ). raise_for_status () # 2. the job; the Idempotency-Key makes a retried POST return the same job job = call ( " POST " , " /jobs " , json = { " uploadId " : upload [ " uploadId " ], " options " : options }, headers = { " Idempotency-Key " : str ( uuid . uuid4 ())}) # 3. poll until the job leaves queued/processing while job [ " status " ] in ( " queued " , " processing " ): time . sleep ( 0.5 ) job = call ( " GET " , f " /jobs/ { job [ ' id ' ] } " ) if job [ " status " ] != " succeeded " : raise BlinkimgError ( f " job { job [ ' status ' ] } : { job . get ( ' error ' ) } " ) link = call ( " GET " , f " /jobs/ { job [ ' id ' ] } /result " ) out = dest_dir / link [ " filename " ] out . write_bytes ( requests . get ( link [ " url " ], timeout = 60 ). content ) return { " file " : out . name , ** job [ " result " ]} if __name__ == " __main__ " : fmt , cap = sys . argv [ 1 ], int ( sys . argv [ 2 ]) out_dir = Path ( " out " ); out_dir . mkdir ( exist_ok = True ) for name in sys . argv [ 3 :]: r = compress ( Path ( name ), out_dir , format = fmt , targetBytes = cap ) print ( f " { name : 15 } { r [ ' inputBytes ' ] : > 9 , } -> { r [ ' outputBytes ' ] : > 7 , } B " f " { r [ ' outputFormat ' ] : 5 } { r [ ' width ' ] } x { r [ ' height ' ] } " f " saved { r [ ' savedPercent ' ] } % { r [ ' file ' ] } " ) Three choices in it are deliberate. One Session . The requests docs say a session reuses the underlying TCP connection to the same host ( requests: Session objects ). The polling loop makes several calls per file, so that saves a handshake each time. A timeout on every call. By default requests do not time out unless you set one ( requests: Timeouts ). A script that runs overnight should never hang on one socket. An Idempotency-Key on the job. The API accepts this header on POST /v1/jobs . If you add a retry around that call and keep the same key, a repeated POST returns the first job instead of creating (and charging for) a second one. What did it print? export BLINKIMG_KEY = bk_... python blinkimg_compress.py avif 100000 photo.jpg photo.png screenshot.png python blinkimg_compress.py jpeg 50000 photo.jpg photo.jpg 576,828 -> 93,922 B avif 1920x1280 saved 83.7% photo.avif photo.png 4,096,344 -> 93,922 B avif 1920x1280 saved 97.7% photo.avif screenshot.png 1,121,126 -> 99,028 B avif 2880x1800 saved 91.2% screenshot.avif photo.jpg 576,828 -> 48,734 B jpeg 1920x1280 saved 91.6% photo.jpg Input Bytes in Job options Bytes out photo.jpg, 1920 × 1280 576.8 KB avif, targetBytes 100000 93.9 KB photo.png, same photo 4,096.3 KB avif, targetBytes 100000 93.9 KB screenshot.png, 2880 × 1800 1,121.1 KB avif, targetBytes 100000 99.0 KB photo.jpg 576.8 KB jpeg, targetBytes 50000 48.7 KB Every output landed under its cap. The JPEG and the PNG of the same photo gave AVIFs of the same size, 93,922 bytes: the encoder sees the same pixels. And the 50 KB JPEG run matches the 48.7 KB the site publishes for that photo; how the site measures explains where its numbers come from. Note: The upload url points at object storage, not at the API. That is why the client PUTs with plain requests.put and not with the session: the session carries your Bearer key, and the key has no business going to the storage host. Send only the bytes there. What does an error look like? Every API error has the same body: {"error": {"code", "message", "requestId"}} . The call() helper turns it into one exception. With a wrong key (the message text came from my local stand-in; the code is the API's): __main__.BlinkimgError: 401 UNAUTHORIZED: bad key The codes you will meet most in a batch script are UNAUTHORIZED , FILE_TOO_LARGE , INSUFFICIENT_CREDITS and RATE_LIMITED . A 429 also carries a Retry-After header; sleep that many seconds and try again. Keyed requests are shaped at 120 writes a minute. What does it cost? Compressing an image costs 1 credit; converting it to another format costs 2. Every account gets 500 free credits a month. The four runs above were three conversions and one compress, so 7 credits on the real service. How I measured Machine: Apple M1 Pro (8 cores), macOS, 2026-10-17. Python 3.9.6, requests 2.32.5 in a fresh venv. Files: photo.jpg , photo.png and screenshot.png from the site's reference set ( apps/web/assets/reference/ ). The API calls ran against a local stand-in of /v1 that I wrote from the API's published request and response contract ( packages/shared/src/api/uploads.ts and jobs.ts ), with the Blinkimg engine ( processImage , the code the workers run) doing every encode. The byte counts are the engine's; the error body shape and codes come from the API's own schema. What I did not test I did not call the production api.blinkimg.com with a live key for this article, so I report no network timings. I did not test batches, /zip or retries under a real 429. I build Blinkimg , an image compressor and converter with a developer API . I wrote this article with help from an AI assistant (Claude), which ran the code on my machine; every number in it comes from those runs.

title: Where an e-commerce explainer video belongs, and what to show in it
author: Bhavesh Vaghela
summary: Most online shops add a video the same way they add a banner: somewhere on the home page, because that is where the space is. The video then gets a few views, no one measures it, and the team decides video "doesn't work". The problem is usually placement and content, not the medium. Here is how I decide both when a store asks me to animate something. Put it where the doubt is A shopper does not need a video everywhere. They need it at the exact point where they hesitate. In a store that is usually one of three places. The product page of a product that is hard to judge from photos. Anything with a mechanism, a size relationship or a setup step: a 20-second clip showing it in use answers questions the photo gallery cannot. This is the highest-value spot, and it is the one most stores skip. The cart or checkout step, for a policy that causes drop-off. If shoppers abandon because they are unsure about returns, delivery windows or subscription cancellation, a short plain explanation beside that step does more than a longer FAQ page. The first ad touch. For paid social, the video is the ad. Here the rules are different: the first two seconds must carry the point, and it must work with the sound off. The home page hero is the last place I would start. Visitors there have not decided what they care about yet, so the video has nothing specific to answer. What to show, in order Whatever the placement, the structure that holds up is short: The situation the shopper recognises. One concrete sentence or scene, not a brand intro. "You measured twice and it still did not fit" beats a logo animation. The product doing the thing. Show the product in use as early as the first third of the video. One proof point. A real number, a real detail, a real customer line. Not three claims, one. The next step, spoken plainly. Where to click, what happens after. Cut anything that does not serve one of those four. Most first drafts are twice as long as they need to be. Length and format For a product page, 15 to 30 seconds is plenty. For a policy or how-it-works clip, up to 45. For ads, render a 9:16 and a 1:1 from the same project so you do not rebuild it for each platform. Always add captions, since a large share of shoppers watch muted. Measure one thing Pick the single number the video is supposed to move before it ships: add-to-cart rate on that product, checkout completion, or click-through on the ad. Compare the pages with and without it for a couple of weeks. If it does not move that number, fix the placement or the opening seconds before blaming the format. I wrote a longer version of this, with examples by product type, here: https://vaghelabhavesh.com/blog/ecommerce-explainer-video-guide.html

title: 356 impressions, 1 click at position 11: is it the title or the ranking?
author: Silkline
summary: I have a page that Google shows a lot and nobody clicks. It's an explainer for the .pkpass file format, the file Apple Wallet uses for boarding passes and tickets. In the last 28 days it had 356 impressions and 1 click. Average position: 11.4. The searches behind it are short and vague: pkpass , .pkpass , pkpass file , .pkpass file . The same site's homepage, ranking 8.7, got 26 clicks from 365 impressions. Another page at 9.4 got 9 from 139. So the site can get clicks. This page can't. What I've tried Two title changes, one at a time. Each time only the title and meta description changed; the heading, body and URL stayed the same: When Title Impressions Clicks Avg position Oct 7–18 PKPASS File Format: What Is a .pkpass File? 126 0 12.0 Oct 20–31 What Is a .pkpass File? How to Open One 201 1 11.2 From Nov 2 What Is a .pkpass File? Open It Free, No App — — — The second title gained impressions and kept the old queries, so the third one builds on it. One click isn't a result, though. It's noise. What I can't tell apart There are three explanations and they need different fixes: Position 11 is page two for most people. If that's it, no title will help, and I should be building links to this page instead. The intent doesn't match. Someone typing pkpass might be a developer looking for Apple's docs, or someone with a ticket that won't open. A "what is" title speaks to neither of them strongly. The title is just weak. Then the third version should show it within a few weeks. Search Console gives me averages, which makes this harder. "Position 11.4" could be 8 on desktop and 14 on mobile, and the click could come from either. My plan is to leave the November 2 title alone until November 30 and compare the same length of time. In the meantime, new links go to the pkpass file page instead of the homepage. What I'd like to know When a page sits around position 10–12 with near-zero CTR, what has moved it for you: the title, the content, or links? How long do you leave a title before judging it on this little traffic? Do you split impressions by device or country before deciding, or is that overthinking a few hundred impressions? I'll come back with the November numbers.

title: LLM Cost Tracking: Per Request, Feature and User (2026)
author: scorpion4ik26-lang
summary: I am the founder of PromptUnit. This post first appeared on the PromptUnit blog , where it is kept up to date. LLM cost tracking means recording what every model call costs, together with the feature, user, model and environment that caused it, so you can see where AI spend comes from and act on it. Without it, cost work is guesswork. Most teams start with a monthly invoice from OpenAI or Anthropic and no visibility beneath that number. The invoice tells you what you spent. It does not tell you which feature drove the spike last Tuesday, which model is responsible for 70% of your bill, or whether your costs grow in step with your users or faster. This guide covers what to track, a cost function you can copy, how to get cost per user, the tools that can do it for you, and what to do when costs move. Provider prices, spend limits and tool features were checked on October 30, 2026. The Core Metrics to Track Cost per feature The most actionable dimension for engineering teams. When you can see that Feature A costs $0.008 per call and Feature B costs $0.47 per call, you know where to focus. This requires tagging every LLM call with the feature that generated it, in your logging code or with a request header if you use a proxy. LLM cost attribution by feature shows what OpenAI and Anthropic can and cannot group by, and how to tag requests. Cost per user (or tenant) For SaaS products, per-user LLM cost is the base of your unit economics. If your average customer generates $12/month in LLM costs but pays you $29/month, your AI margin is thin. If one customer generates $200/month in costs, the monthly invoice will not tell you who it is. The per-user section below has the queries. User-level cost tracking also supports fair-use policies, per-plan rate limits and pricing decisions. Model distribution What share of your calls goes to each model? If 90% of calls go to your most expensive model, check whether every one of them needs it. If you recently moved some traffic to a cheaper model, model distribution tells you whether the change is working as intended. Tracking model distribution over time also surfaces drift: as new features ship, they may default to an expensive model without going through a cost review. Task type breakdown Which task types are most common in your traffic? What is the average cost per task type? Tasks that are both high-volume and simple are the first place to test a cheaper model. Cost per environment Separate tracking for production, staging and development is basic hygiene. A cost spike in development (a developer testing with a long context window, a test suite making more calls than expected) should not stay invisible until the invoice arrives. Cache hit rate Cached input is billed at a fraction of the normal input price, so the share of input tokens read from the cache moves your bill. OpenAI's prompt caching guide suggests dividing total cached tokens by total input tokens and grouping by user, workspace or day. A drop often means something near the start of the prompt began changing between calls. Prompt caching on OpenAI and Anthropic covers how each provider caches. Latency by model Cost and latency are related. Smaller models are often faster. Tracking latency per model per task type shows user-facing performance next to cost when you decide which model a feature should use. Setting Up Cost Monitoring Option 1: Log every call with one cost function The basic approach: every LLM call is logged with its cost and metadata when it is made. The cost has to come from the usage object the provider returns, priced per model, and it has to handle cached tokens. OpenAI and Anthropic report cached tokens differently. In OpenAI's Responses API, input_tokens includes the tokens read from the cache and the tokens written to it. In Anthropic's Messages API, input_tokens counts only the tokens after the last cache breakpoint, and cache reads and writes come in separate fields. A function that ignores this overstates the cost of cached calls on OpenAI and understates it on Anthropic. from datetime import datetime , timezone # USD per 1M tokens, standard tier, from each provider's pricing page on October 16, 2026. # OpenAI rows are for prompts up to 272K input tokens. # Claude Haiku 5.5 row is for prompts up to 100,000 tokens. # Claude cache_write is the 5-minute cache; 1-hour cache writes cost more. PRICES = { " gpt-6.1-sol " : { " input " : 2.00 , " cached " : 0.10 , " cache_write " : 2.50 , " output " : 10.00 }, " gpt-6-sol " : { " input " : 2.00 , " cached " : 0.20 , " cache_write " : 2.50 , " output " : 10.00 }, " gpt-6-luna " : { " input " : 0.10 , " cached " : 0.01 , " cache_write " : 0.125 , " output " : 0.50 }, " claude-sonnet-5-5 " : { " input " : 2.00 , " cached " : 0.10 , " cache_write " : 2.50 , " output " : 10.00 }, " claude-haiku-5-5 " : { " input " : 0.10 , " cached " : 0.01 , " cache_write " : 0.125 , " output " : 0.50 }, } def cost_usd ( provider : str , model : str , usage ) -> float : p = PRICES [ model ] # KeyError on purpose: an unknown model must not be logged at $0 if provider == " openai " : # Responses API: input_tokens includes cached and cache-write tokens. # output_tokens includes reasoning tokens, which are billed as output. details = usage . input_tokens_details cached = details . cached_tokens or 0 written = getattr ( details , " cache_write_tokens " , 0 ) or 0 uncached = usage . input_tokens - cached - written elif provider == " anthropic " : # Messages API: input_tokens counts only tokens after the last cache breakpoint. cached = usage . cache_read_input_tokens or 0 written = usage . cache_creation_input_tokens or 0 uncached = usage . input_tokens else : raise ValueError ( f " no usage mapping for { provider } " ) return ( uncached * p [ " input " ] + cached * p [ " cached " ] + written * p [ " cache_write " ] + usage . output_tokens * p [ " output " ] ) / 1_000_000 def log_call ( provider : str , model : str , response , feature : str , user_id : str ) -> None : log_event ({ " ts " : datetime . now ( timezone . utc ). isoformat (), " provider " : provider , " model " : model , " feature " : feature , " user_id " : user_id , " usage " : response . usage . model_dump (), # raw counts, for later analysis " cost_usd " : cost_usd ( provider , model , response . usage ), }) The prices come from OpenAI's pricing page and Anthropic's pricing page . Our price pages for GPT-6.1 Sol , GPT-6 Sol , GPT-6 Luna , Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 show today's numbers. An example of why the cache fields matter: a Claude Sonnet 5.5 call with 10,000 input tokens read from the cache, 2,000 uncached input tokens and 500 output tokens costs (2,000 x $2.00 + 10,000 x $0.10 + 500 x $10.00) / 1,000,000 = $0.0100. The same call with no cache would cost (12,000 x $2.00 + 500 x $10.00) / 1,000,000 = $0.0290. Keep the price table in one place and update it when prices change. Long prompts are priced higher on some models (over 272K input tokens on OpenAI's newer models, over 100,000 tokens on Claude Haiku 5.5), so add those tiers if your prompts get that long. This approach works, but every call site must pass the feature and the user. It is easy to miss one. Option 2: A wrapper that every call goes through A better approach is to make the wrapper the only way your app calls a model, so no call is made without attribution: class TrackedClient : """ The only path to the model, so no call goes unlogged. """ def __init__ ( self , client , feature : str ): self . client = client self . feature = feature def respond ( self , user_id : str , model : str , ** kwargs ): response = self . client . responses . create ( model = model , ** kwargs ) log_call ( " openai " , model , response , self . feature , user_id ) return response summaries = TrackedClient ( openai_client , feature = " ticket-summary " ) Option 3: A proxy or gateway A proxy or gateway sits in the request path and records every call, so there is no logging code at each call site. You change the API base URL and send the feature or user as request headers. Helicone's AI Gateway, the LiteLLM proxy and PromptUnit work this way; the tools table below shows what each one records. The trade-off is one more service between your app and the provider. How to Track LLM Cost per User Provider usage reports are built around your account structure, not the users of your app. Anthropic's usage report, for example, groups by API key, workspace, model and a few service settings, not by the user a request was made for. Per-user cost has to come from your own logs or from a tool that reads a user id from each request. 1. Pass a user id with every call. Use your internal user id (a UUID from your database), not an email address. In your own logs it is a column, as in the log_call function above. If you use a gateway, send it the way the gateway expects: Helicone reads the Helicone-User-Id header, LiteLLM reads the x-litellm-customer-id header or the request's user field, and Langfuse takes a userId on traces. One user action in an agent can make several model calls, so log the same id on all of them. The multi-agent cost spiral explains why those calls add up. 2. Group by user and day. With calls stored in a table such as llm_calls (ts, user_id, feature, model, cost_usd) , this Postgres query gives daily cost per user for the last 30 days: SELECT user_id , date_trunc ( 'day' , ts ) AS day , count ( * ) AS calls , round ( sum ( cost_usd ):: numeric , 4 ) AS spend_usd FROM llm_calls WHERE ts >= now () - interval '30 days' GROUP BY user_id , day ORDER BY day DESC , spend_usd DESC ; 3. Compare with what the user pays. Join to your users and plans to see AI cost as a share of each paying user's price: SELECT c . user_id , u . plan , p . monthly_price_usd , round ( sum ( c . cost_usd ):: numeric , 2 ) AS ai_cost_30d , round (( 100 * sum ( c . cost_usd ) / p . monthly_price_usd ):: numeric , 1 ) AS pct_of_price FROM llm_calls c JOIN users u ON u . id = c . user_id JOIN plans p ON p . name = u . plan WHERE c . ts >= now () - interval '30 days' AND p . monthly_price_usd > 0 GROUP BY c . user_id , u . plan , p . monthly_price_usd ORDER BY pct_of_price DESC LIMIT 20 ; A user on a $29 plan with $12 of AI cost in 30 days spends 41% of their price on AI alone (12 / 29). Free users have no price to divide by, so list them separately, sorted by cost. Pick a threshold that fits your margins and review everyone above it. AI cost per user covers how to set that threshold from your revenue per user. Best LLM Cost Tracking Tools in 2026 Each option below reports LLM cost. They differ in how they get the data, how finely they can split it, and whether they can stop spending or only report it. Every cell comes from the tool's own documentation, checked October 16, 2026. PromptUnit is our product, and its row lists only what this post documents. Tool Per user Per feature or tag Budget enforcement How it captures data Langfuse userId on traces; cost aggregated per user Tags and metadata; dashboards can split cost by tag Alerts on cost thresholds, filterable by user or tag; it is not in the request path, so it does not block calls SDKs (OpenTelemetry based) send traces in the background Helicone Helicone-User-Id header Helicone-Property-[Name] headers Cost-based rate limits per user or per property ( Helicone-RateLimit-Policy with u=cents ), plus cost alerts AI Gateway (change the base URL), or its Manual Logger LiteLLM proxy x-litellm-customer-id header or the user field; also internal users and teams Tags via the x-litellm-tags header, request metadata or the virtual key max_budget per virtual key, internal user, team, customer and tag; calls over budget are rejected A proxy you run, with a database for spend logs Provider consoles (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) Only with one key, project or workspace per user Only with one key, project or workspace per feature Monthly hard limits per organization or project (OpenAI), per workspace (Anthropic), per project (Google, experimental) Built in; nothing to install PromptUnit No per-user view x-promptunit-feature header; requests are also grouped into your app's steps Not covered in this post Proxy: two settings (API base URL and a PromptUnit key); your provider key stays Sources: Langfuse cost tracking , users , tags and alerts ; Helicone header directory , custom properties , rate limits and alerts ; LiteLLM customers , tag budgets , budgets and spend tracking ; OpenAI spend limits , Anthropic workspaces , Gemini API billing . How to choose: if you need to stop one user's or one feature's spending, Helicone's cost-based rate limits and LiteLLM's budgets do it in the request path. Langfuse alerts you but leaves the call alone. The provider consoles cap a whole project or workspace. For a closer look at two of these, see PromptUnit vs Helicone and PromptUnit vs Langfuse . Alerting Setup Cost tracking is only useful if anomalies surface in time to act. The providers cover the first alert type below: OpenAI sends spend alerts at amounts you set on its Limits page, and Anthropic can alert when a workspace's spending reaches thresholds you set. The other two need your own logs or a tool from the table above. Absolute cost threshold Alert when spend in the current billing period exceeds a fixed dollar amount. Set it at 80% of your expected monthly budget. Alert: Monthly LLM spend has exceeded $4,000 (80% of $5,000 budget) Percentage increase vs rolling average Alert when daily or hourly cost is well above the rolling 7-day or 30-day average. This catches spikes that do not hit absolute thresholds but show that something changed. Alert: LLM spend in the last 1 hour is 3.2x the 7-day hourly average This type of alert is most effective for catching unexpected traffic increases, runaway loops, or new features calling expensive models at high volume. Per-feature cost anomaly Alert when a specific feature's cost per call rises sharply. A 5x increase in cost per call for a feature usually points to a prompt change, a context window change, or a model change that was not cost-reviewed. Alert: Feature "document_analysis" average cost per call increased 4.7x (from $0.023 to $0.108) in the last 24 hours Cost Anomaly Detection Common causes of unexpected cost spikes: New feature launched without a cost estimate. A feature that generates long outputs, uses a long context window, or chains several model calls can cost many times more per call than a typical feature. If cost estimation is not part of the feature review, the first signal is the invoice. Prompt change increased output length. A prompt that used to produce 200-token responses now produces 800-token responses after an edit. Output tokens cost more than input tokens on every major provider: five times on OpenAI's GPT-6 models (for prompts up to 272K tokens) and six times on GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-5.4, five times on Anthropic's current Claude models, and from five times on Gemini 3.8 Flash to about eight times on Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite . OpenAI bills reasoning tokens as output, and Google's output price includes thinking tokens. So output length has an outsized effect on cost. Context window growth over time. For multi-turn conversation features, context grows with each turn. A conversation that started at 500 tokens per call may be at 8,000 tokens after 20 turns. If your application does not trim or summarize conversation history, per-call cost keeps growing over a session. Model change without a cost review. Moving a feature from GPT-6 Luna to GPT-6.1 Sol, or from Claude Haiku 5.5 to Claude Sonnet 5.5, multiplies the per-token price by 20 on both input and output ($0.10 to $2.00 per million input tokens, $0.50 to $10.00 per million output tokens). If cost monitoring does not flag the change, it stays invisible until the invoice. Runaway agent loop. Agent workflows that call tools and retry can make far more model calls than planned. A bug that makes an agent loop, or a task harder than the retry budget assumed, can multiply the call count. For a way to turn calls and tokens into a monthly bill, see OpenAI API Cost Too High? Six Fixes, Ordered by Effort . For what defaulting to one expensive model costs beyond the invoice, see The Hidden Cost of Defaulting to Your Flagship Model . Budget Enforcement Tracking tells you what happened. Enforcement stops it from happening again. Provider spend limits All three large providers let you cap monthly spend, but none of them does it per API key: OpenAI: a monthly spend limit for the whole organization or for one project. With "Enforce a hard limit" on, requests over the limit get a 429 error with the code organization_spend_limit_exceeded or project_spend_limit_exceeded . Enforcement is not instant, so recorded spend can slightly exceed the limit. ( OpenAI spend limits ) Anthropic: a monthly spend limit per workspace, set in the Claude Console under Settings > Workspaces. It can be lower than the organization's limit but not higher, and the Default Workspace cannot have its own limit. ( Anthropic workspaces ) Google: a monthly spend cap per project, set on the Spend page in AI Studio. Google marks it as experimental and says spend can run past the cap for about 10 minutes while billing data catches up. Billing accounts on paid tiers also have a monthly cap ($250 on Tier 1, for example); when it is reached, all linked projects pause until the 1st of the next month. ( Gemini API billing ) The risk: one cap covers everything in the project or workspace, so a single runaway feature can block every other feature that shares it. Giving each critical feature its own project or workspace limits the damage. Per-feature limits Enforce limits at the feature level in your application or gateway. A feature expected to make 10,000 calls a day at $0.05 per call should stop accepting new requests after 12,000 calls. LiteLLM's tag budgets and Helicone's per-property rate limits do this in a gateway. Per-user spending limits For multi-tenant or consumer-facing products, enforce a per-user LLM spend limit. A single power user who generates 100x the average LLM traffic is an economics problem. Helicone can limit spend per user with Helicone-RateLimit-Policy using u=cents and s=user , and LiteLLM can give each customer a max_budget . Or check the per-user total from your own logs before each call. Pre-call cost estimation Before making a model call, estimate the expected cost from the input token count and the model. If the estimate exceeds a threshold, reject the request, use a cheaper model, or ask for explicit confirmation. From Tracking to Cost Management LLM cost management is the loop that turns tracking data into lower or more predictable bills. It has four steps: Track. Log every call with its cost, feature, user and model, using the cost function above or a tool from the table. Alert. Set a provider spend alert at 80% of the monthly budget, and a spike alert on your own data for cost per hour and cost per call by feature. Cap. Put hard limits at the provider for each project or workspace, and per-user or per-feature budgets in your code or gateway. Review. Once a week, sort features and users by spend and look at the top three of each. For each one, decide whether the prompt can be shorter, whether caching would help, whether a cheaper model holds up on that task (test it on your own traffic first), or whether the plan price needs to change. LLM Observability: The Metrics That Actually Drive Decisions covers the other metrics worth watching next to cost. Where PromptUnit Fits PromptUnit checks each request, and when a cheaper model is just as good for that request, it uses that model; otherwise the request goes to the model you asked for. Setup is two settings: point your app's AI API base URL at it and add your PromptUnit key. Your own provider key stays. For cost tracking, the dashboard shows the cost of every request and breaks cost down per model, and per feature when you tag requests with the optional x-promptunit-feature header (letters, digits, underscore, hyphen and dot, up to 64 characters). It also groups requests into the steps of your app or agent and shows what each step costs. PromptUnit has no per-user view, so keep per-user cost in your own logs with the queries above. In Privacy mode only what billing needs is stored (the models, tokens, cost and response time), so feature names and steps are not kept. See Also OpenAI API Cost Too High? Six Fixes, Ordered by Effort The Hidden Cost of Defaulting to Your Flagship Model LLM Cost Attribution by Feature AI Cost Per User PromptUnit vs Helicone PromptUnit vs Langfuse Try It Free See where your AI budget goes. PromptUnit's dashboard shows every request with the model that answered and what it cost. It is free until it has saved you money, then it takes 20% of what it saves. Start free . FAQ What is LLM cost tracking? Recording what each model call costs, together with the feature, user, model and environment behind it. The provider invoice gives you one total. Tracking per request shows which feature or user drives the spend and whether cost grows faster than usage. What is the difference between LLM cost tracking and LLM cost management? Tracking tells you where the money went. Cost management is what you do with that data: alerts before the budget runs out, hard caps at the provider or in a gateway, and a regular review of the top features and users by spend. How do I track LLM cost per user? Send your internal user id with every call, compute each call's cost from the usage object the provider returns, and store both. Then group by user and day in SQL and compare each user's 30-day cost with the price of their plan. Gateways such as Helicone and LiteLLM can group by a user id header for you. Can I set a hard spending limit on OpenAI, Anthropic or Google? Yes, but not per API key. OpenAI sets monthly hard limits per organization or per project, Anthropic sets monthly spend limits per workspace, and Google lets you set a monthly spend cap per project in AI Studio, a feature it marks as experimental. Checked October 16, 2026. How much more do output tokens cost than input tokens? For prompts up to 272K tokens, five times on OpenAI's GPT-6 models and six times on GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-5.4. Five times on Anthropic's current Claude models. On Google it runs from five times (Gemini 3.8 Flash) to about eight times (Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite). Checked November 5, 2026.

title: Building Songfetti: How I Made Personalized Songs Work Entirely in the Browser
author: AI Predictions Dev
summary: Most "personalized gift" apps feel like a black box. You type a name, click submit, wait three seconds, and get a generic jingle. It works, but it feels cold. I wanted to build something warmer: a tool that takes a name and a few specific memories and turns them into a genuine, heartfelt song. But I also hated the friction of server-side processing. If I wanted this to feel instant and private, it had to run locally. Songfetti is the result. It’s a lightweight web app that generates custom songs using AI, but everything happens right in your browser. No waiting for a server response, no uploading your personal memories to a cloud database. Just type, listen, and share. Here is how I approached the architecture and why local processing mattered more than I initially thought. The Constraint: Privacy and Latency My primary goal was simplicity for the user, which meant minimizing steps. Traditional AI audio pipelines often involve sending text prompts to an API, waiting for a response, fetching audio files, and rendering them. This introduces latency and privacy concerns. If a user is typing intimate memories ("My daughter loves dinosaurs," or "Our first trip to Kyoto"), they shouldn't have to worry about where that data goes. By keeping the inference engine on-device, I removed the network bottleneck. The app loads a compact model directly into the browser’s memory. When the user inputs their name and memories, the text is tokenized and processed immediately. The audio generation happens in real-time. For a short, personalized track, this means the transition from "input" to "playback" is nearly seamless. It feels less like a cloud service and more like a native app feature. Handling Multilingual Output Without Heavy Assets One of the trickier parts was supporting multiple languages without bloating the bundle size. If I shipped separate models for English, Spanish, French, and Japanese, the initial load time would suffer. Instead, I utilized a multilingual foundation model that handles tokenization and phonetic mapping across languages efficiently. The logic is straightforward but requires careful tuning. When a user enters a name and memories, the app parses the phonetic structure of the name to ensure the melody aligns with natural speech rhythms. For example, a two-syllable name needs a different melodic contour than a four-syllable name to sound natural. The model analyzes the input text’s syllabic stress and matches it to the generated melody. This ensures that even if the song is sung in Japanese or Portuguese, the vocals don’t sound robotic or misaligned with the beat. I focused heavily on the "preview" experience. The first 15 seconds of the song are generated instantly. This is crucial because users need to know if the tone matches their intent before committing to the full track. By optimizing the inference steps for the initial segment, the app provides immediate feedback. If the user likes the vibe, the full track renders in the background while they review the lyrics. This parallel processing keeps the UI responsive. Why Local Execution Changes the Experience There is a psychological benefit to local processing that I didn’t anticipate. Because the app responds instantly, users are more likely to tweak their inputs. They’ll change "loves hiking" to "loves hiking with her dog" and hear the difference in seconds. This iterative loop is where the personalization actually happens. In server-heavy apps, the delay between input and output breaks this flow. Users tend to accept the first result. With Songfetti, the low friction encourages refinement. The visual design reflects this speed. The interface is minimal: a text area for the name, a text area for memories, and a large play button. There are no complex settings or style selectors. The AI handles the stylistic choices based on the emotional tone detected in the memories. If the memories are happy and concise, the tempo increases. If they are reflective, the melody slows down. This automation reduces decision fatigue for the user. Lessons from Shipping a Lightweight AI Tool Building Songfetti taught me that "fast" is a feature, not just a metric. Users don’t care about the underlying architecture; they care about how quickly their idea becomes reality. By pushing the compute to the client, I traded a bit of initial load time for a much smoother interaction loop. The bundle size is kept tight by using optimized WASM modules for the inference engine, ensuring it runs smoothly even on older laptops. Another lesson was about transparency. Since the processing is local, I made sure the UI clearly indicates when generation is happening. Simple visual cues, like a pulsing waveform during generation, help users understand the system state without needing complex loading spinners. It feels more like a conversation than a transaction. If you’re building similar tools, I’d be curious to hear your thoughts. Do you find that on-device processing significantly improves the perceived quality of interaction in your own projects, or do you prefer the raw power of server-side models?
